## The Claim

John Stockton reportedly had a resting heart rate near 35 beats per minute. In the context of an NBA career that produced 1,504 regular-season games over 19 seasons — the most in league history at his retirement — a number that specific invites scrutiny. If an unusually low resting heart rate reflects genuinely superior cardiovascular adaptation, we should expect some trace in the box score: fewer missed games than peers, steadier late-game decision-making, and a shot selection that holds up under accumulated fatigue.

This post asks whether that trace is detectable — not whether it is caused by cardiovascular physiology. The analysis uses permutation inference throughout, comparing Stockton to 14 matched point-guard contemporaries who met the same career-length threshold. The methodology follows [a companion analysis of Boris Diaw](../diaw-35bpm/index.qmd), who shares the same reported resting heart rate and whose case was the cleaner test: Diaw played entirely within the BRef play-by-play era, the sourcing on his 35 BPM figure is better documented, and no age-regime caveat applies to his prime career. Stockton is the harder, earlier, and in some ways more famous version of the same question.

**Sourcing note.** The 35 BPM figure for Diaw comes from multiple post-retirement interviews and is well-attested. The equivalent figure for Stockton appears in circulation but is less directly documented. The analysis below treats it as a prior — a physiological claim consistent enough to motivate a box-score test — not as an established fact.

---

## Who to Compare Stockton To

The reference class is point guards who debuted between 1984 and 2001, played at least 600 career games, and averaged at least 28 minutes per game. Fifteen players meet this threshold, including three — Isiah Thomas, Kevin Johnson, and Tim Hardaway — who retired before the BRef play-by-play era (1996-97 onward), and others like Jason Kidd and Steve Nash who overlapped with Stockton's final seasons.

| Player | Career | Active Games | Years |

| John Stockton | 1984–2003 | 1,504 | 19 |
| Gary Payton | 1990–2007 | 1,335 | 17 |
| Mark Jackson | 1987–2004 | 1,296 | 17 |
| Terry Porter | 1985–2003 | 1,274 | 17 |
| Jason Kidd | 1994–2013 | 1,391 | 19 |
| Isiah Thomas | 1981–1994 | 979 | 13 |
| Sherman Douglas | 1989–1999 | 686 | 10 |
| Mookie Blaylock | 1989–2002 | 889 | 13 |
| Steve Nash | 1996–2014 | 1,217 | 18 |
| Tim Hardaway | 1989–2003 | 867 | 13 |
| Rod Strickland | 1988–2005 | 1,094 | 17 |
| Muggsy Bogues | 1987–2001 | 889 | 14 |
| Kenny Anderson | 1991–2005 | 858 | 14 |
| Derek Harper | 1983–1999 | 1,199 | 16 |
| Kevin Johnson | 1987–2000 | 735 | 12 |

All players selected on ≥ 600 games — this is a selection on the dependent variable for E1. The estimand is durability *among players who completed a long career*, not among all drafted point guards.

## Did He Actually Miss Fewer Games? (E1 — full career 1984–2003)

::: {#cell-fig-e1-pg .cell execution_count=2}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Career games missed per 82 — PG cohort. Stockton marked in orange.](index_files/figure-html/fig-e1-pg-output-1.png){#fig-e1-pg fig-alt='Dot plot of games missed per 82-game season for Stockton and 14 PG comparators. Stockton sits at the far left with 1.18 games missed per 82.'}
:::
:::


Stockton missed 1.18 games per 82 over his career — the lowest figure in the reference class, at the 6.7th percentile of the 15-player distribution. The next closest is Gary Payton at 1.63 games per 82. The permutation null (5,000 reassignments of the "treated" label across cohort members) places the observed gap at p = 0.194, two-sided. With n = 15, the minimum achievable two-sided p is approximately 0.13 — so the result is near the floor of what is detectable with this cohort size.

That is an honest framing of a genuine finding. Stockton sits at an extreme of the durability distribution. The permutation test cannot rule out chance with conventional thresholds because the reference class is small — not because the result is ambiguous. For instance, Kevin Johnson's 20.75 games missed per 82 compared to Stockton's 1.18 represents a 17.5-game gap across a full career; that magnitude is large regardless of a p-value. The appropriate inference is that Stockton's durability is *consistent with* unusually robust physical maintenance rather than injury luck or schedule protection, while acknowledging that the evidence alone cannot distinguish between the two.

**Season correction.** Games-missed-per-82 denominators are adjusted for shortened seasons: 1999 (50 games), 2012 (66 games), 2020 (65 games), 2021 (72 games).

## Does Shot Selection Hold Up on Back-to-Back Nights? (E3 — full career)

::: {#cell-fig-e3-pg .cell execution_count=3}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Shot selection shift on back-to-back games vs rest — PG cohort. Each point is a player; Stockton labeled.](index_files/figure-html/fig-e3-pg-output-1.png){#fig-e3-pg fig-alt='Scatter of B2B minus rest differences in 3PA/FGA (x-axis) and FTA/FGA (y-axis) for each PG cohort player. Stockton sits in the lower-right corner, showing the largest decline in FTA/FGA with a near-flat 3PA/FGA shift.'}
:::
:::


On back-to-back nights, Stockton's three-point attempt rate is essentially flat relative to rested games (Δ = +0.002, d = 0.17, 67th percentile of cohort). His free-throw attempt rate, on the other hand, drops by 0.049 per field-goal attempt — the largest such decline in the reference class (6.7th percentile, d = −1.62). Compared to rest days, Stockton draws fewer fouls per shot on consecutive-game nights. This is consistent with a behavioral adaptation: less aggressive attacking on tired legs, or a more conservative approach to contact. It is not direct evidence of physical advantage — it could equally reflect score-margin effects, opponent fouling strategy, or reduced game-script exposure to foul-drawing situations.

For context, Kevin Johnson shows a similar FTA/FGA decline on B2B nights (−0.037), as does Muggsy Bogues (−0.039). The cohort pattern is not Stockton-specific; what distinguishes him is the magnitude. A Cohen's d of −1.62 is a large effect by conventional benchmarks — though those benchmarks were calibrated on study populations far larger than 15.

**Conditioning caveat.** Back-to-back games select healthier player-states — players who were healthy enough to play the first game are already a non-random subset. Within-player pairing removes stable player effects but not state selection.

---

## Within-Game Resilience: 1996–2003 Window (Stockton ages 34–40)

**Data limitation.** BRef play-by-play starts 1996-97. Stockton's first 12 seasons (1984–96) have no quarter data in the publicly available record. Outreach to Squared Statistics (Justin Jacobs), who has video-reconstructed pre-1996 quarter logs, is pending; that data would extend the within-game window to Stockton's prime years.

**Age-regime caveat.** This analysis covers Stockton at ages 34–40. His career peak — where a cardiovascular advantage would theoretically matter most — falls outside the observable window. A null result here does not contradict a prime-career resilience claim. These are different estimands at different biological ages; conflating them would be a mistake in either direction.

::: {#cell-fig-e2-pg .cell execution_count=4}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![E2: FT% by quarter — Stockton vs PG cohort, 1996–2003. Left: full cohort mean per quarter. Right: Stockton.](index_files/figure-html/fig-e2-pg-output-1.png){#fig-e2-pg fig-alt='Bar charts of mean free throw percentage by quarter for the four-player 1996–2003 window. Stockton\'s Q4 bar is the highest in his panel (0.836), while the cohort panel shows decline or flatness in Q4.'}
:::
:::


In the seven seasons where quarter-level play-by-play data exists (1996–97 through 2002–03), Stockton's Q4 free throw percentage is 0.836 — 4.1 percentage points *higher* than his Q1–Q3 average of 0.795. Among the three contemporaries for whom the same window was available (Payton, Jackson, Harper), Harper shows the sharpest Q4 degradation (−19.6 pp, from 0.773 to 0.577), while Payton and Jackson hold flat (+0.7 and +0.3 pp respectively). Stockton is the only player in the four-person window whose Q4 free throw shooting improves.

The mixed-effects interaction coefficient (Q4 × is_treated) is +0.0504 (p = 0.494, two-sided permutation, n = 5,000). With four players in the analysis window, the minimum achievable two-sided p is approximately 0.50 — the result is at the floor of what the test can detect. The p-value reflects sample size more than effect size: Stockton occupies the favorable extreme of a four-player distribution, and the test cannot rule out chance at conventional thresholds given n = 4. The directional finding — the only player whose late-game free throw shooting holds up or improves — is the appropriate takeaway.

The blowout-game sensitivity (restricted to Q4 margin ≤ 10) could not be run: only 18 player-quarter observations had score margin data available, below the minimum for stable estimation.

::: {#cell-fig-e4-pg .cell execution_count=5}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![E4: AST/TOV by quarter — Stockton vs PG cohort, 1996–2003. Note: per-quarter AST/TOV is numerically unstable (52% of quarter observations have zero turnovers); this figure is included for completeness but the coefficient estimate is unreliable.](index_files/figure-html/fig-e4-pg-output-1.png){#fig-e4-pg fig-alt='Bar charts of AST/TOV ratio by quarter. The y-axis scale is distorted by zero-turnover quarter-game observations, which blow up the ratio.'}
:::
:::


E4 (AST/TOV in Q4) and E5 (TS% in Q4) are not interpretable at per-quarter BRef resolution in this window. In 52% of player-quarter observations the turnover count is zero — a normal outcome for any single quarter — which makes the ratio numerically undefined and drives the mixed-effects interaction coefficient to an implausible 128. The estimand is valid in principle but requires aggregation at half-game or full-game resolution to be usable. TS% coverage is even thinner: only 21% of player-quarter rows have non-null values, because a player who attempts no field goals in a quarter contributes nothing to the efficiency estimate. The model reaches a degenerate solution (coef = 0.000, p = 1.000). Both estimands require either coarser aggregation or a minimum-minutes filter that would further reduce a window already limited to four players and seven seasons.

### Confounders for within-game estimands

| Confounder | Direction | Mitigation |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Score margin (blowout) | Starters sit; compresses Q4 estimates toward zero | Sensitivity: restricted to games with Q4 margin ≤ 10 |
| Intentional fouling | Inflates FTA in close games; FT% reflects pressure context | FT% (E2) is least-confounded metric |
| Timeout availability | Coaches use Q4 timeouts strategically for recovery | Stated explicitly; not mitigated |
| Age regime (34–40) | Later-career Stockton; null ≠ no prime-career effect | Stated explicitly in every result |

## What the Data Can and Cannot Say

**Selection bias.** The cohort conditions on ≥ 600 career games. Players who missed substantial time due to injury early in their careers are excluded. E1 describes durability among those who *made it to* long careers — not durability as a draw from the full population of drafted point guards.

**Sourcing asymmetry.** The 35 BPM figure for Diaw is well-documented from interviews. The equivalent claim about Stockton circulates without the same evidentiary trail. This post treats both as motivating hypotheses rather than established facts, which is appropriate — the box-score test would be worth running even if the specific physiological mechanism were different.

**Causal language.** No result here proves the 35 BPM claim, disproves it, or establishes that cardiovascular physiology *caused* the observed box-score patterns. The correct framing is: Stockton's durability record is *consistent with* the physiological hypothesis and *does not contradict* it. The data cannot distinguish between true cardiovascular advantage, favorable injury luck, conservative roster management by the Jazz, or selection on player type.

**Pre-1996 gap.** E2/E4/E5 cover 7 of Stockton's 19 seasons. Any claim about his full-career within-game resilience requires either Jacobs's video-reconstructed data or an explicit acknowledgment that the observable window covers only the final third of his career at declining biological age.

---

## Conclusion

John Stockton's career durability record — 1.18 games missed per 82 over 19 seasons — sits at the far end of a 15-player reference class of matched point-guard contemporaries. The permutation test places this at p = 0.194, which is near the floor of what is detectable with a cohort of this size; it is not evidence of chance so much as evidence of a small sample. His free-throw attempt rate on back-to-back nights drops more than any other player in the cohort (Δ = −0.049 per FGA, d = −1.62), consistent with a protective behavioral pattern under fatigue — though the causal mechanism is indeterminate from the data.

Within-game, the picture is constrained. The 1996–2003 quarter-split window covers four players with data available (Stockton, Payton, Jackson, Harper). Among them, Stockton is the only player whose Q4 free throw percentage *improves* relative to his own Q1–Q3 average (+4.1 pp), while Harper degrades sharply (−19.6 pp) and the others hold flat. The full Q1→Q4 profile reinforces this: Stockton's free throw percentage rises monotonically across all four quarters (76.9% → 80.6% → 83.2% → 84.7%) — a pattern none of the other three players share. The permutation p (0.494) is at the floor of what a four-player test can detect, so the inference is directional rather than inferential — consistent with late-game resilience, but not a statistical claim in the conventional sense. E4 (AST/TOV) and E5 (TS%) are not interpretable at per-quarter resolution: half of all quarter-level observations have zero turnovers, and TS% coverage is too sparse for the model to converge. Both require coarser aggregation than BRef quarter splits provide.

The Diaw case — where full-career quarter data is available, the sourcing is cleaner, and the analysis runs without the age-regime qualification — is the more direct test of the 35 BPM hypothesis. This post is the harder version: a longer career, a shorter observable window, and a claim that is harder to trace to its source. What the data can say is this: Stockton's career durability is at the far end of a 15-player reference class, his B2B shot selection shows the largest protective shift in the cohort, and his Q4 free throw shooting does not degrade in the one window where it is observable. None of those findings prove the physiological claim. Together, they do not contradict it.
